evaluation.positioning_hook: A bullied teen battling binge eating, family shame, and first love spirals toward a breaking point when his closest friend’s trauma and his own self-loathing collide.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: There is a clear emotional lane here — adolescent shame, body image, first love, and family rejection — that can connect with viewers who respond to intimate coming-of-age drama. The material is hard to position broadly, though, because the script’s strongest scenes are also its most abrasive and the current execution is uneven.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The core premise is legible early: Kevin is a teen whose eating disorder, social humiliation, and home life are all collapsing at once. What blurs the hook is that the script keeps adding new threads without a single clean dramatic engine to organize them.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Kevin has a usable central contradiction — defensive, lonely, funny, ashamed — and Claire gives him a real counterpoint. But most of the supporting characters are sketched as functions or provocations rather than fully durable people, so the cast doesn’t yet generate much lift beyond the lead.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script is willing to go into uncomfortable territory around binge eating, religious shame, queer hostility, and sexual trauma, which gives it a harder edge than a standard teen drama. The downside is that the boldness often arrives as blunt declaration rather than a more controlled dramatic shape.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The opening school/home beats establish Kevin’s misery, but the script repeatedly stalls into conversation scenes and explanatory passages instead of escalating through decisive turns. The Act 3 section is especially underbuilt, arriving as a writer’s note rather than a dramatized climax.

resonant_originality.reasoning: A teen male lead with binge-eating shame, religious family pressure, and queer-adjacent social fallout is a fresh combination. The individual ingredients are interesting, but the script hasn’t yet fused them into something that feels inevitable and singular.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The school, home, and friend-group worlds are recognizable, but they are mostly containers for dialogue rather than textured systems with their own rules and pressures. The clearest texture comes from Jackie’s religious household and the cafeteria/social hierarchy, but it’s still thin.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script swings between earnest teen drama, blunt social issue writing, and occasional dark-comic banter, but it doesn’t yet settle into a stable tonal identity. The result is emotionally direct, but not especially controlled or distinctive.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real seeds here — body image, family ideology, friendship betrayal, trauma, and identity conflict — that suggest a deeper emotional story underneath the surface. Right now, though, the script states most of its depth outright instead of letting it accumulate through behavior and subtext.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Kevin/Mike and Kevin/Claire each have usable chemistry, and Jackie provides a strong source of conflict. But the relationships are still mostly one-note pressure points, so the ensemble doesn’t yet feel like a system that can keep generating new story on its own.

lead_characters.name: Kevin
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage male, high-school age, likely mid-to-late teens.
lead_characters.hook: Kevin is a lonely, defensive teen whose binge eating, shame, and need for connection keep colliding in public and at home. He wants love and belonging, but he keeps sabotaging both with anger, denial, and self-loathing; the role lives in that contradiction, and the script gives him a raw, messy interiority that can anchor the whole film.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea — a wounded, volatile young lead who has to carry pain, humor, and embarrassment in the same scene. It gives an actor a full emotional instrument panel: shame spirals, outbursts, tenderness, and the chance to make an unsympathetic behavior feel human.

lead_characters.name: Claire
lead_characters.hook: Claire is Kevin’s first real romantic possibility and the one person who speaks openly about her own eating disorder history. She reads as confident, alternative, and emotionally direct, but the script uses her more as a mirror and catalyst than as a fully independent engine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 or Olivia Cooke in The Quiet Ones a chance to be both cool and deeply vulnerable. The appeal is the mix of edge and confession — a character who can pivot from flirtation to painful honesty in a beat.

lead_characters.name: Mike
lead_characters.hook: Mike is Kevin’s closest friend, the one who sees him clearly enough to challenge him but still wants to stay in his orbit. The script gives him a painful backstory and a lot of emotional weight, but he functions more as a pressure valve and victim of the story than as a fully shaped co-engine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of emotionally loaded supporting turn that made Lucas Jade Zumann in 20th Century Women or Justice Smith in The Get Down memorable — a sensitive friend role with real hurt under the surface. It offers the chance to play loyalty, longing, and damage without needing to dominate the film.

lead_characters.name: Jackie
lead_characters.hook: Jackie is a strict, religious, controlling mother whose love is filtered through discipline, shame, and fear. She’s one of the script’s clearest sources of conflict because she can be funny, cruel, and sincerely worried all at once.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Patricia Clarkson did in Sharp Objects or Melissa Leo in The Fighter — authority with emotional damage underneath. The part offers sharp scene work, moral rigidity, and the chance to complicate a potentially one-dimensional parent.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.hook: David is the protective, judgmental parent who immediately reads Kevin as a threat and polices the relationship. He’s more functional than layered on the page, but he gives the film a clean external obstacle and a social pressure point.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid character-actor territory in the vein of a Michael Stuhlbarg or Shea Whigham supporting turn — a father role that can turn a dinner scene into a power struggle. The appeal is in playing suspicion, control, and barely contained disapproval.

lead_characters.name: Lily
lead_characters.hook: Lily is the softer counterweight in Claire’s house, more open and less reactive than David. She’s not deeply developed, but she helps define the family atmosphere and gives the dinner scene some warmth and friction.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded supporting role that can land like a Laura Linney or Amy Ryan scene turn — a parent who communicates volumes in a few lines. It gives an actor the chance to play concern without becoming the obvious antagonist.

lead_characters.name: Ben
lead_characters.hook: Ben is one of Kevin’s school antagonists, built as a blunt social threat and body-shamer. He’s not layered, but he helps establish the public humiliation pressure around Kevin.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact bully role — the kind that lets a young actor make a memorable impression fast, similar to early-career turns in teen dramas where the job is to be instantly legible and hateable.

lead_characters.name: Stephanie
lead_characters.hook: Stephanie is Ben’s partner in social cruelty and another face of the school’s judgmental ecosystem. Like Ben, she’s more a pressure function than a full person, but she helps create the film’s public-shame texture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sharp, scene-efficient teen antagonist part — the kind that gives an actor a chance to play social dominance and cruelty with precision. It’s a useful showcase for timing and attitude.

lead_characters.name: Ms. Williams
lead_characters.hook: Ms. Williams is the authority figure who escalates Kevin’s conflict from embarrassment into institutional punishment. She’s mostly procedural in function, but she gives the school world a face and a consequence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is dependable authority-role material in the lane of a strong TV guest turn — a chance to play bureaucratic firmness and controlled frustration. It’s not flashy, but it’s clean scene work.

lead_characters.name: Ms. Platty
lead_characters.hook: Ms. Platty is a brief institutional presence in ISS, mostly there to mark Kevin’s punishment and isolation. The role is thin, but it contributes to the sense that school is another place where Kevin is managed rather than understood.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small but usable character part for an actor who can make authority feel specific with very little screen time. It’s the kind of role that can still register if played with exactness.

lead_characters.name: Mr. Jones
lead_characters.hook: Mr. Jones is the classroom authority who sets the academic stakes early and then recedes. He’s functional, but he helps establish Kevin’s failure loop and the pressure of school as another arena of judgment.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a straightforward teacher role with enough authority to matter in a scene. It’s the kind of part that gives an actor a clean, no-nonsense presence.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: specialty theatrical or streaming original.

budget.note: Contemporary school, home, and club interiors with no VFX or set-piece action keep this inside a contained indie footprint.

casting.note: Kevin has to carry shame, anger, romantic awkwardness, and eating-disorder material without losing audience sympathy, which narrows the lead search more than the scale suggests.

development.note: The script’s Act 3 is presented as a prose outline rather than dramatized scenes, and the Mike trauma thread plus Kevin/Claire breakup material would need a much firmer dramatic shape before a buyer could assess the finished film.

comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the teen outsider perspective, emotional confession, and school/social shame lane, with a lead who experiences the world as a pressure cooker.

comp_set.title: The Spectacular Now
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the messy teen romance and self-destructive behavior playing against a grounded high-school setting.

comp_set.title: Short Term 12

audience_target.primary_audience: Viewers who respond to intimate, emotionally raw teen dramas about shame, identity, and first love.
audience_target.demographics: Primarily 16-34, with a female skew and strong overlap among indie-drama audiences and viewers drawn to mental-health and coming-of-age material.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary interiors, a small teen ensemble, and no visible VFX or action set pieces point to a contained indie feature.

types_of_buyers: specialty distributors looking for youth-skewing emotional drama
streamer original-film teams building out the prestige teen lane
indie producers seeking a low-cost, actor-forward character piece
festival-minded buyers looking for a raw social-issue debut feature
lane_fit.detail: The script sits naturally in the intimate, actor-driven teen-drama lane: school humiliation, family pressure, and first-love stakes all play in a contained contemporary world. Its commercial appeal is strongest where buyers want emotional honesty over plot machinery.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with no clear sequel or spinoff vector; the supporting characters are not built with enough independent depth to support a franchise extension.

strengths.what_it_means: That gives the film a clear emotional center buyers can understand immediately, which is the difference between a generic teen drama and a lead-role showcase. It’s the kind of part that attracts young actors looking for a painful, sympathetic breakout.
strengths.evidence: Kevin eating the snacks alone, crying in his room, then later admitting he binged and feels fat.

strengths.what_it_means: Binge eating in a male teen lead is a less crowded lane than the usual high-school insecurity material, which makes the premise more ownable in a crowded market. Buyers chasing issue-driven indie drama will notice the specificity even when the execution is rough.
strengths.evidence: Kevin’s online eating-disorder test, the OMAD diet talk, and his repeated self-labeling as overweight.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Claire gives the story a romantic counterweight.
strengths.what_it_means: The relationship creates a second commercial hook beyond the disorder material: first love with emotional stakes and a shared vulnerability. That helps the film speak to teen-drama buyers who need a relationship spine, not just a social issue.
strengths.evidence: The dinner confession scene where Claire admits anorexia and then asks Kevin how he feels about her.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jackie is a strong conflict source.
strengths.what_it_means: The religious, controlling mother gives the film a clear home-life antagonist and a recognizable audience entry point around family shame. That kind of parent role can elevate the project if cast well, because it creates scenes that are playable rather than purely expositional.
strengths.evidence: Jackie’s prayer, the snack confrontation, the slap, and the homophobic exchange.

strengths.what_it_means: A contemporary, mostly interior, small-cast feature is easier to finance and schedule than a broader teen ensemble movie. That makes the script attractive to buyers who want a contained indie with emotional stakes rather than a costly youth ensemble.
strengths.evidence: School, home, bedroom, cafeteria, and one club sequence with no VFX or major action.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, actor-forward indie drama with a clear emotional hook: a teen boy’s binge-eating shame collides with first love, family control, and social humiliation. The production footprint is small enough for specialty or streamer buyers, and the lead role has the kind of messy, vulnerable showcase that can attract a breakout performance.

items.detail: The script stops at a prose summary of what the third act 'basically' should be, which means the buyer is not seeing the actual climax, reversals, or emotional payoff on the page. That is the sharpest development issue here because it prevents a real greenlight read on the film’s ending.

items.area: The trauma material is extremely sensitive.
items.detail: Mike’s sexual-abuse backstory and the later rape scene are the most severe content elements in the script, and they materially narrow the buyer conversation. Even in mature lanes, that material will trigger a harder legal, ratings, and taste discussion than the rest of the film.

items.area: The script leans on direct statement over drama.
items.detail: Kevin’s internal thoughts are repeatedly spelled out in monologue-like text, and several scenes explain the emotional point instead of letting behavior carry it. That keeps the film from feeling fully cinematic yet and is a noticeable craft friction for buyers reading for execution.

Mike, Claire, Jackie, and the school antagonists all have usable functions, but only Jackie has much scene-specific force; the rest often read as catalysts rather than fully dimensional people. That limits relationship density and makes the film more dependent on Kevin alone than the material needs to be.

items.area: The brand and music references need a pass.
items.detail: Metallica, Korn, Nirvana, AC/DC, and Christian music are all named in the script, so a production would need to decide whether those references stay as written or are cleared/replaced. None of them are deal-breakers individually, but they are real clearance items if the film keeps the current dialogue.

issues.headline: The biggest friction is structural: the film does not yet present a dramatized third act, so the ending conversation is still hypothetical rather than evaluable. Beyond that, the script’s most intense material — especially the sexual-violence thread and the heavy reliance on internal explanation — will make buyers read it as a development project, not a ready package.
